cells.tense: The pen is in your hand now and the framework is taking its shape in front of you.
cells.act: distinguish what is yours from what you borrowed
cells.ask: Take a claim you'd defend in a room and trace where you picked it up and why you kept it. Keep whatever holds up as yours, and set the rest down for now.
cells.core:
Somewhere in shared meaning, one of the frameworks you keep and hand on gets examined. That gets tested in company — a claim your circle wants kept in shape, and you can say what you actually think of it. What holds is knowing several things fully rather than one thing loudly. The declarations carry because you can hear the other readings of them.

There's a version of this that's been going for a while and you may not have named it: more than one thing is true in what you hold, and the ordinary room wants only one. When the whole thing gets pulled one way — a practice half the room keeps, an old custom with a new question under it — the habit is to force it shut, and the forcing is what makes it feel like a fight. Do the smaller move first: separate the parts. Take a claim you did not choose and trace where you chose it.
cells.sheetLine: You hold more than one truth and still say yours.
cells.verb: Declaring a framework outward before it has deepened
cells.place: Standing in the shared meaning and tradition a community carries forward

cells.tense: You are bracing for a version of the shared story that has not been written yet.
cells.act: go all the way into the pattern until you meet its edge
cells.ask: Pick a rule you hold about how a shared practice should run and follow it down until it stops making sense. Name where it runs out, then hold there for a few days before you patch anything.
cells.core:
Where the framework has to be declared outward, the declaration is arriving before the thing it declares has been lived with. People get the whole structure of how something should run before anyone knows what is being organized. The bracing does this — it writes the rules first so the future cannot surprise you. The plan nobody asked for is what comes back.

A way through: take a rule you hold about how the shared work should go, and follow it all the way down until it runs out. The pattern you polish at night has an edge, and the edge is worth more than the polish. Name where it stops working, then hold there longer than feels comfortable. The point isn't to finish it. The edge is where the next real thing starts.
cells.sheetLine: You write the rules before you know who's playing.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door you have not walked through and it is already behind you.
cells.act: commit to the long build and do today's part
cells.ask: Start building a practice you want to stand in your shared life, ten minutes of it today. Do whatever piece can be done now, and let tomorrow wait.
cells.core:
In the common meaning, there is a stand you have not taken. The framework that would organize things is not on the table, and the people who look to you for a word get quiet agreement instead. What should be clear is not being said, and its absence is doing its own work — as a hole pulls water the way a hand would not.

This is less about nerve and more about the thing built. A practice in a shared life is not a speech; it is a series of small days spent on it until it stands. That is what confidence looks like from the inside — someone continuing a thing past the point where it was exciting. So pick what you would build if you were going to build it, and do today's piece. One afternoon won't finish it, and it is supposed to be a long build.

cells.tense: The pen is down and the writing is still happening through you in the room.
cells.ask: Count what something the community already went through handed you — an old fight, a ritual nobody canceled. Write the list, read it once, then put it away.
cells.core:
You are the one who keeps the shared thing standing — quietly, before anyone asks, by instinct — and your own telling says you just show up. Something in how the group does things still holds because you carry the shape of it. The way you describe yourself is that of a participant. The actual thing is closer to a load-bearing wall.

Here is the smaller version: not a position or a public claim, just looking at what these years in it have already grown. Gather it. Pick an ending that already happened in the group and count what it left behind — the actual yield, not the official version. The instinct will be to wave the list off as obvious, or to keep it and say nothing. Keep it for yourself first; being the one who carried a thing is worth seeing as yours.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the shared thing standing and call it showing up.
cells.verb: Declaring a framework outward before it has deepened
cells.place: Standing in the shared meaning and tradition a community carries forward

attempts.check: The draft's riskiest move is the Too Much cell, where I claim the person is rehearsing a framework before it has content; the record only supports bracing, not the motive — a reader could say the tidying and editing is just care. Too Little is the other risk: I locate them behind the present without saying what put them there, which the rules permit but a reader may want filled in. The asks all survive being wrong — any of the four acts is useful even if the read misses, because each one is something the person does rather than something done to them. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the Too Much sheet line, 'You're drafting rules for a document that isn't yours yet' — it is neat, and neatness is what I have to watch here.
